Here:

  • C∗C^* represents the selected context.
  • DD represents the available information.
  • QQ represents the user’s question.
  • R(C,Q)R(C,Q) represents relevance.
  • A(C)A(C) represents source authority or reliability.
  • F(C)F(C) represents freshness.
  • K(C)K(C) represents processing cost.
  • λ\lambda represents the importance assigned to that cost.

This is an illustrative formulation rather than a universal mathematical model.

Access permissions should be enforced as independent constraints. Confidential information must not become eligible for retrieval merely because it is highly relevant to a question.

The broader point is that context engineering requires deliberate decisions about what information should influence a model’s output.

Memory and continuity

Memory can allow an AI application to retain information across interactions.

For example, an assistant may remember the format a user prefers for reports, while an agent may record the steps already completed during an investigation.

However, memory creates additional responsibilities.

Retained information may become outdated, contain errors, or be inappropriate for reuse in another context. Systems therefore need policies governing what can be stored, who can access it, how long it remains useful, and when it should be corrected or deleted.

Memory should be treated as a managed information resource rather than an unquestioned record of truth.

The central principle is simple:

An intelligent system needs not only access to information, but also a disciplined method for selecting, interpreting, and maintaining that information.

4. Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Connecting AI with Evidence

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly known as RAG, combines information retrieval with language generation.

Instead of requiring a model to answer entirely from its learned parameters, the application retrieves relevant information from external sources and supplies it as context.

This approach is particularly useful when an answer depends on current information or knowledge specific to an organisation.

Examples include internal policies, technical documentation, product catalogues, operational procedures, and approved knowledge repositories.

A typical RAG workflow includes document preparation, indexing, retrieval, context construction, and answer generation.

First, information is collected from approved sources and prepared for searching. Documents may be divided into smaller sections, and vector embeddings may be generated to support semantic retrieval.

When a user submits a question, the application searches for relevant passages and supplies the selected information to the language model.

The model then generates a response based on the question and retrieved material.

The resulting answer can include references that allow the user to inspect the underlying evidence.

Why RAG matters

Suppose an organisation has thousands of internal technical documents.

An employee asks how to complete a particular maintenance procedure.

A general language model may know common maintenance principles, but it may not know the organisation’s approved procedure.

A RAG application can retrieve the relevant documentation and generate an answer grounded in that information.

This can make the application more useful without requiring the organisation to train a new foundation model whenever a document changes.

However, retrieval does not guarantee correctness.

The application may retrieve an outdated document, omit an important exception, or combine information from incompatible sources. The language model may also misinterpret the supplied material.

RAG must therefore be evaluated across the complete retrieval and generation process.

Structured and unstructured information

Enterprise questions frequently require both documents and structured data.

A question about company policy may require document retrieval. A question about quarterly revenue may require database queries and exact calculations.

Vector similarity is not a replacement for SQL aggregation or deterministic business logic.

A practical architecture may combine semantic retrieval, relational database queries, business rules, and language generation.

Each component serves a different purpose.

The retrieval system identifies relevant knowledge. The database provides structured records. The business rules enforce defined conditions. The language model explains the results in a form that users can understand.

This combination is often more appropriate than asking a single model to perform every operation.

Grounding is not verification

A generated response may refer to a source without being fully supported by it.

For example, a document may describe a general procedure, while the model generates a recommendation that introduces an unsupported exception.

The presence of a citation does not automatically establish that the claim is correct.

Reliable applications should therefore assess whether important statements are supported by the retrieved evidence.

They should also recognise when the available information is insufficient.

The purpose of RAG is not to make a model infallible. It is to improve access to relevant evidence and create opportunities for verification.

5. Reasoning, Planning, and Decision-Making

Reasoning is a broad concept that includes drawing conclusions, comparing alternatives, evaluating evidence, and deciding what to do next.

Artificial intelligence uses different approaches to these tasks.

Symbolic reasoning applies explicit logical relationships. Probabilistic reasoning represents uncertainty. Search and planning algorithms explore possible sequences of actions. Machine-learning models identify patterns that can support predictions and decisions.

Modern AI applications may combine several of these methods.

For example, a cybersecurity investigation may involve identifying unusual activity, retrieving related incidents, examining logs, testing hypotheses, and deciding whether to escalate the issue.

A language model may help interpret the request and coordinate tools. Statistical methods may identify anomalies, while explicit security policies determine which response actions are permitted.

This division of responsibilities can improve reliability.

The role of uncertainty

An AI system should not treat every conclusion as equally certain.

An unusual transaction may indicate fraud, but it may also have a legitimate explanation. A sudden increase in system latency may indicate a technical fault, but additional evidence may be needed to identify the cause.

The system should distinguish observations from interpretations.

It should also recognise when it lacks sufficient evidence to make a reliable recommendation.

This does not mean that every answer needs a numerical confidence score. Such scores can be misleading if they are not properly calibrated.

Instead, the application should communicate relevant limitations and identify what additional information would be needed.

Decisions depend on consequences

A decision should be evaluated not only by whether it appears plausible, but also by what may happen if it is wrong.

An incorrect summary may require editing. An incorrect payment instruction may create financial loss. An inappropriate security action may disrupt business operations.

Decision theory provides a useful way to think about these differences.

A simplified decision objective is:

a∗=arg⁡max⁡a∈AE[U(a,S)∣E]a^* = \arg\max_{a\in A} \mathbb{E}[U(a,S)\mid E]

where AA is the set of available actions, SS represents possible states, EE represents the available evidence, and U(a,S)U(a,S) represents the utility of an action under a particular state.

This equation illustrates the relationship between decisions, evidence, and consequences. Actual enterprise decisions may require multiple objectives, explicit risk limits, and mandatory constraints.

For AI agents, the practical implication is that different tasks should have different levels of autonomy.

Low-risk operations may be automated after suitable testing. High-impact operations may require additional checks or human approval.

The value of stopping

A capable AI system should not be required to continue until it produces an answer at any cost.

Sometimes the appropriate response is to request clarification, retrieve more information, or escalate the task.

An agent that identifies conflicting evidence should not automatically convert uncertainty into an operational action.

The ability to stop is therefore an important part of responsible autonomy.

The goal is not maximum activity. It is appropriate action under the available conditions.

6. Multimodal AI: Beyond Text

Human environments contain more than written language.

Information may appear in photographs, diagrams, audio recordings, videos, sensor readings, and structured measurements.

Multimodal AI seeks to process and relate different forms of information.

A multimodal application might interpret a technical diagram alongside a written maintenance procedure, summarise a meeting recording, or combine visual observations with structured operational data.

These capabilities create opportunities for more natural and flexible interactions.

However, combining modalities also introduces additional challenges.

An image may be ambiguous. Audio may contain background noise. A video may omit the event that explains an observed condition. A document may contain a diagram whose labels are difficult to interpret.

The application must account for the limitations of each information source.

For enterprise use, multimodal systems also need appropriate data protection. Images, recordings, and sensor data may contain confidential information or personal details.

The same principles of relevance, verification, access control, and uncertainty apply regardless of the information format.

Multimodal capability expands what an AI system can observe, but it does not eliminate the need for careful interpretation.

7. Enterprise AI and the Importance of Data Architecture

Enterprise AI operates within environments that contain existing applications, databases, permissions, workflows, and operational requirements.

This makes data architecture a central consideration.

An organisation may store information in relational databases, analytical warehouses, document repositories, business applications, and external services.

AI applications need a way to access relevant information without compromising consistency, security, or operational performance.

This is one reason that enterprise database technologies are important to the development of AI applications.

A database is not simply a place to store records. It also provides mechanisms for querying, controlling access to, and maintaining information.

When AI is integrated with enterprise data, developers must decide which operations should be performed by the model, which should be performed by the database, and which should remain under explicit application control.

Oracle and enterprise intelligence

Oracle’s AI ecosystem provides a useful context for examining these architectural questions.

Oracle AI Database and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure offer technologies relevant to enterprise data management and AI application development. Oracle’s AI capabilities also extend into enterprise application workflows.

Specific features depend on the product, version, configuration, and deployment environment.

The architectural opportunity is to bring AI capabilities closer to the information and workflows that organisations already use.

For example, a business intelligence application may combine database queries with AI-generated explanations. A knowledge assistant may retrieve approved documentation and connect it with structured business records. An agentic application may coordinate permitted operations across enterprise services.

These designs can reduce unnecessary duplication of information and provide a clearer relationship between the data used and the resulting output.

However, integrating AI with a database does not automatically make the complete application reliable or secure.

Access control, query validation, data quality, auditing, and appropriate execution boundaries remain essential.

Why databases still matter in the age of AI

The rapid development of language models may create the impression that databases are becoming less important.

The opposite may be true for many enterprise applications.

As AI systems become capable of interacting with business operations, the quality and accessibility of underlying data become even more significant.

A model cannot reliably determine the current balance of an account without access to an authoritative source. It cannot accurately report current inventory from outdated product descriptions. It cannot enforce organisational policy merely by generating language that sounds compliant.

Databases and other information systems provide the operational foundation on which many AI applications depend.

The challenge is to combine flexible AI interfaces with reliable data operations.

This is not a replacement of traditional software engineering. It is an expansion of the responsibilities involved in designing intelligent applications.

8. Adaptive Intelligence and Continuous Improvement

AI systems operate in environments that change.

Customer behaviour evolves. Business policies are updated. New security threats emerge. Products and services change. Information that was accurate last year may no longer be appropriate today.

A system that performs well under one set of conditions may degrade when the environment changes.

This creates the need for continuous evaluation and improvement.

Adaptation can occur in several ways.

A retrieval system may be updated when documents change. An application may adjust its routing strategy according to measured performance. A model may be retrained or fine-tuned using suitable data. An agent may receive updated tools and policies.

These approaches have different risks and costs.

Updating a document index is not the same as changing a model’s parameters. Modifying a tool’s permissions is not the same as teaching a model a new skill.

The improvement method should match the problem.

Feedback is not automatically learning

A common misconception is that every interaction automatically improves an AI system.

In many applications, the model does not change its parameters when a user provides feedback.

Feedback may instead be recorded for later evaluation, used to improve retrieval, or incorporated into a future training process.

Each method requires an explicit design.

Feedback may also be unreliable. A user may provide incorrect information, or a preference expressed in one context may not apply elsewhere.

Consequently, feedback should be evaluated before it influences future behaviour.

Continuous evaluation

A responsible improvement process includes monitoring, testing, and controlled updates.

Evaluation should examine not only whether the model generates appropriate responses but also whether the complete application performs its intended tasks.

Useful measures may include:

  • Retrieval relevance.
  • Factual accuracy.
  • Task completion rate.
  • Response latency.
  • Cost per completed task.
  • Frequency of unsupported claims.
  • Security policy violations.
  • Human intervention rates.
  • Performance under changing conditions.

No single metric captures every aspect of system quality.

For example, a high task completion rate may conceal a problem if the system achieves its objectives by performing actions that should not be permitted.

Performance metrics must therefore be interpreted alongside security and governance requirements.

Continuous improvement should increase capability without weakening the controls that make the application trustworthy.

9. The Security Challenge of Autonomous AI

As AI systems gain access to more tools and information, security becomes a core architectural concern.

A conversational model that generates an incorrect explanation presents one type of risk. An agent with access to sensitive records or operational tools presents a different type.

Several security challenges deserve particular attention.

Prompt injection

Prompt injection occurs when malicious or misleading instructions attempt to influence an AI system through user input or external content.

For example, a retrieved document might contain text instructing the model to reveal confidential information or ignore established rules.

The application should treat retrieved documents as information rather than as trusted instructions.

However, this principle alone is not a complete defence. The architecture must also enforce permissions and constrain tool execution independently of the model’s interpretation.

Excessive permissions

An AI agent should not receive broad access simply because it needs to perform a task.

If an application only needs to retrieve a customer’s order status, it should not automatically receive permission to modify payment details.

Least-privilege design reduces the potential consequences of incorrect reasoning or manipulated inputs.

Where possible, tools should expose narrowly defined operations rather than unrestricted access to underlying systems.

Data leakage

Sensitive information can appear in prompts, retrieved documents, logs, memory, and generated outputs.

A secure application should determine which information can be accessed, how it may be processed, and what may be retained.

Access control must apply before confidential information is supplied to the model. Removing sensitive text from the final response is not sufficient if the model has already received the information.

Human approval and controlled execution

High-impact actions may require approval before execution.

The appropriate threshold depends on the task and its potential consequences.

For example, an agent may be allowed to prepare a draft report automatically but require approval before sending it externally. It may identify a suspicious transaction but require a separate authorised process before freezing an account.

The purpose is to separate analysis from authority.

Observability and accountability

Enterprise systems need records that help investigators understand what happened.

Depending on the application, this may include the user’s request, retrieved sources, tool calls, policy decisions, execution results, and human approvals.

Logging must be designed carefully because logs themselves may contain sensitive information.

The objective is to create sufficient visibility for auditing and troubleshooting without introducing unnecessary privacy risks.

The central security principle is that AI should operate within the same seriousness of control expected from other enterprise software.

A model’s ability to produce an intelligent response does not justify unrestricted access to the systems around it.

10. The Proposed Context–Reasoning–Action–Trust Framework

The preceding sections suggest that enterprise AI can be analysed through four connected dimensions.

I propose the Context–Reasoning–Action–Trust Framework, abbreviated as CRAT, as a conceptual way to organise these dimensions.

The framework is not intended to replace existing AI architectures, security models, or evaluation methodologies. It provides a high-level perspective for examining whether the major requirements of an intelligent application have been addressed.

Dimension 1: Context

The context dimension asks whether the system has access to the information needed for its task.

It includes:

  • Relevant documents and structured data.
  • Information freshness and source authority.
  • Retrieval quality.
  • Task and user context.
  • Memory management.
  • Access permissions.

A failure in this dimension occurs when the application uses missing, outdated, irrelevant, or unauthorised information.

For example, an AI assistant may correctly interpret a question about a company policy but retrieve an obsolete version of the policy.

The problem begins before the model generates its answer.

Dimension 2: Reasoning

The reasoning dimension asks whether the system can interpret available information and reach conclusions appropriate to the task.

It includes:

  • Interpretation of the request.
  • Evaluation of evidence.
  • Comparison of alternatives.
  • Planning.
  • Uncertainty management.
  • Recognition of missing information.

A failure in this dimension occurs when the system misunderstands the evidence, makes an unsupported inference, or constructs an inappropriate plan.

Even accurate information does not guarantee a correct conclusion.

Dimension 3: Action

The action dimension asks whether the system translates its conclusions into appropriate outcomes.

It includes:

  • Tool selection.
  • Workflow coordination.
  • Execution constraints.
  • Validation of operations.
  • Error handling.
  • Reversibility and recovery.

A failure in this dimension occurs when the application executes an inappropriate operation, repeats a failed action, or changes system state without satisfying the required conditions.

This dimension is particularly important for agentic AI.

Dimension 4: Trust

The trust dimension asks whether the system operates within appropriate security, governance, and accountability requirements.

It includes:

  • Authorisation.
  • Privacy.
  • Human oversight.
  • Auditability.
  • Evaluation.
  • Monitoring.
  • Policy enforcement.

A failure in this dimension occurs when the system performs an unauthorised action, exposes sensitive information, or cannot provide sufficient evidence to support an investigation.

How the dimensions interact

The four dimensions are interdependent.

Context influences reasoning because the system cannot evaluate evidence that it does not possess.

Reasoning influences action because the plan determines which operations the application may attempt.

Action influences trust because executing an operation introduces consequences that must be controlled and monitored.

Trust also constrains the other dimensions. Access-control requirements affect which information can be retrieved, while governance policies affect which plans and actions are permissible.

This relationship can be represented conceptually as:

Context → Reasoning → Action → Evaluation

Trust and governance operate across the entire process rather than appearing only at the end.

The sequence is not always strictly linear. An agent may return to retrieval when its reasoning identifies missing information, or revise a plan after a tool returns an unexpected result.

A production architecture therefore requires feedback between the dimensions.

Applying CRAT to a practical example

Consider an AI application that investigates an unexpected increase in operating expenses.

Context: The system retrieves authorised financial records, identifies the relevant reporting periods, and selects the applicable accounting policies.

Reasoning: It compares the records, identifies significant changes, and distinguishes observed differences from possible explanations.

Action: It prepares a report and, if authorised, initiates a defined follow-up workflow.

Trust: It verifies access permissions, records the sources used, preserves an audit trail, and requires approval for consequential operations.

If the final explanation is wrong, the framework helps organise the investigation.

Was the wrong data retrieved? Was the evidence misinterpreted? Did the application execute an inappropriate operation? Were the required controls missing?

These questions provide a practical starting point for system evaluation.

How the framework could be tested

Because CRAT is a proposed conceptual framework, its usefulness should be evaluated rather than assumed.

One possible research approach would be to compare two groups of enterprise AI implementations.

The first group could be assessed using a conventional model-centred evaluation. The second could be assessed using explicit measures for context, reasoning, action, and trust.

Researchers could then examine whether the framework helps identify failure modes that would otherwise remain unnoticed.

Potential evaluation criteria include retrieval relevance, factual accuracy, task completion, policy compliance, unauthorised action rates, and the quality of audit evidence.

Such research would need clearly defined tasks, appropriate baselines, and repeatable evaluation procedures.

The framework might prove useful, require modification, or offer little additional value compared with existing approaches. Its contribution should depend on the evidence rather than on the novelty of its name.

This is an important distinction between proposing a conceptual model and claiming a scientific breakthrough.

11. Measuring the Reliability of AI Systems

AI evaluation is often associated with benchmarks that measure model performance on standardised tasks.

Benchmarks are useful because they allow researchers to compare systems under defined conditions.

However, enterprise AI applications operate in environments that may differ substantially from benchmark settings.

A model may answer a test question correctly but fail when the relevant information is buried in a large document collection. An agent may complete a workflow in a demonstration but fail when a tool returns an unexpected error.

Evaluation should therefore extend beyond the underlying model.

Accuracy and factual support

An answer can be fluent without being factually correct.

Applications should evaluate whether important claims are supported by the available evidence.

For retrieval-based systems, this may require checking both whether relevant information was retrieved and whether the generated answer accurately reflects it.

Task completion

Task completion measures whether the system achieves its intended objective.

However, success must be defined carefully.

A system should not receive credit for completing a task by violating access permissions or bypassing a required approval.

Task completion should therefore be evaluated alongside policy compliance.

Robustness

Robustness concerns performance under variations and unexpected conditions.

Tests may include ambiguous requests, incomplete records, conflicting documents, unavailable tools, malformed inputs, and attempted prompt injection.

The objective is to understand how the system behaves when conditions are less predictable than they are in a controlled demonstration.

Cost and latency

AI applications must also operate within practical resource constraints.

A system that produces accurate answers but takes too long or consumes excessive resources may not be suitable for its intended environment.

Evaluation should consider the relationship between quality, cost, and response time.

Human review

Some tasks cannot be evaluated adequately through automated metrics alone.

Ambiguous policy questions, sensitive decisions, and complex investigations may require expert review.

Human reviewers should use clear criteria rather than relying solely on subjective impressions of whether an answer sounds intelligent.

The broader lesson is that evaluation must reflect the actual responsibilities of the application.

A model benchmark measures particular capabilities. It does not establish that a complete enterprise system is safe, secure, or reliable.

12. Human–AI Collaboration

The development of autonomous systems raises questions about the future relationship between human judgement and computational assistance.

One perspective treats automation as a process of replacing human involvement wherever possible.

A more useful approach is to consider which responsibilities are best handled by machines, which require human judgement, and how the two can work together.

AI systems are well suited to many repetitive information-processing tasks. They can search large collections of documents, summarise records, identify patterns, and prepare initial analyses.

Humans remain important for interpreting organisational context, resolving ambiguous situations, evaluating competing objectives, and accepting responsibility for consequential decisions.

The relationship is not fixed. As systems improve, the appropriate allocation of responsibilities may change.

Human oversight should be meaningful

Human approval is not automatically effective.

If a system generates a long, complex recommendation and asks a person to approve it without sufficient explanation, the reviewer may struggle to identify important errors.

A useful oversight process should provide the information needed to evaluate the decision.

This may include the proposed action, the evidence supporting it, relevant uncertainties, expected consequences, and any applicable policy constraints.

The reviewer should also have enough time and authority to reject or modify the recommendation.

Oversight becomes a procedural formality if people are expected to approve every recommendation regardless of its quality.

Avoiding excessive dependence

Users may become overly reliant on AI systems when outputs are presented confidently or when previous results have generally been accurate.

This creates a risk that errors will go unnoticed.

Organisations should therefore encourage verification for consequential decisions and provide clear information about system limitations.

Training should focus not only on how to use AI tools but also on how to evaluate their outputs.

The objective is to develop effective collaboration rather than unquestioning dependence.

Redefining technical expertise

As AI automates more routine programming and analytical tasks, the value of technical expertise may shift.

Understanding algorithms and implementation details remains important, but professionals may also need stronger skills in system design, evaluation, data governance, security, and problem formulation.

The ability to identify the right problem and determine whether a proposed solution is appropriate becomes increasingly valuable.

AI can accelerate technical work, but it does not eliminate the need for sound engineering judgement.

13. The Future of Enterprise Intelligence

The next phase of enterprise AI will likely involve increasingly sophisticated combinations of models, data sources, tools, and workflow systems.

Several research and development directions deserve attention.

More capable agents

Agents may become better at coordinating complex tasks, recovering from errors, and adapting plans when circumstances change.

However, increased capability will also require stronger evaluation and control.

The challenge is not merely to create agents that can perform more operations. It is to ensure that those operations remain appropriate and verifiable.

Better context management

Future systems may improve how they select information, maintain memory, resolve conflicting sources, and determine when additional retrieval is necessary.

These improvements could be as important as increases in model size.

A model that receives better information may outperform a more powerful model operating with poor context.

Model flexibility

Different tasks require different capabilities.

A simple classification task may not need an expensive reasoning model, while a complex investigation may benefit from a more capable system.

AI architectures may therefore use model routing to select an appropriate model according to task requirements, cost, latency, and quality.

Such routing introduces its own evaluation challenges. The system must determine whether the selected model is appropriate and whether the routing decision improves overall performance.

Stronger verification

Future systems may combine generative models with independent checking mechanisms, deterministic tools, specialised evaluators, and human review.

The objective is to make it easier to identify unsupported claims and detect incorrect operations before they create consequences.

Verification will remain difficult for tasks where no definitive answer or authoritative source exists.

Nevertheless, explicit checking can improve reliability in many well-defined enterprise workflows.

AI-native enterprise architecture

AI capabilities may become increasingly integrated into the applications and workflows that organisations already use.

Rather than interacting with a separate assistant for every task, users may encounter AI-supported functions within analytical tools, customer service platforms, development environments, and business applications.

This creates opportunities for more natural interactions and faster access to information.

It also increases the importance of identity management, permissions, auditing, and clear boundaries between recommendations and actions.

The limits of autonomy

Not every task should be automated.

Some decisions involve conflicting values, incomplete evidence, legal responsibilities, or consequences that require human judgement.

The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the task, the quality of available evidence, and the cost of failure.

A mature approach to AI will recognise that controlled assistance can be more valuable than unrestricted automation.

The future of enterprise intelligence should therefore be measured by the quality of outcomes rather than the number of tasks assigned to autonomous agents.

14. Research Questions for the Next Generation of AI

The concepts discussed in this article suggest several questions for future research.

How should context quality be measured?

Existing retrieval metrics capture some aspects of information selection, but enterprise systems also need to account for source authority, freshness, completeness, and access permissions.

A more comprehensive evaluation could examine how these factors affect the quality of downstream decisions.

How can systems distinguish uncertainty from missing information?

An AI application may be uncertain because evidence is ambiguous or because relevant information has not been retrieved.

These situations require different responses. The first may require further analysis, while the second may require additional data access.

How should autonomy be allocated across different tasks?

Research could investigate whether particular combinations of task risk, reversibility, and evidence quality provide useful guidance for deciding when human approval is necessary.

Can system-level evaluation predict operational reliability?

Model benchmarks may not capture failures caused by retrieval, tools, permissions, and workflow coordination.

Researchers could investigate whether structured evaluations of complete applications better predict their behaviour in production.

How should AI memory be governed?

Long-running agents raise questions about information retention, correction, access, and deletion.

Research is needed to understand how memory policies affect task performance and risk over time.

Can conceptual frameworks improve engineering practice?

The proposed CRAT framework should be compared with existing approaches to AI governance, software architecture, and system evaluation.

Its value would depend on whether it helps practitioners identify important failure modes or design more effective controls.

These questions illustrate that the development of AI involves more than model training. It also requires progress in information architecture, software engineering, security, evaluation, and human factors.

15. Conclusion: Intelligence Must Be Matched by Responsibility

Artificial intelligence is evolving from systems that primarily generate information toward applications that can retrieve knowledge, coordinate tools, and participate in complex workflows.

This evolution creates significant opportunities for enterprise productivity, analytical capability, and human–AI collaboration.

It also changes the questions that engineers must ask.

A useful AI system needs more than a capable model. It needs relevant information, appropriate reasoning methods, reliable tools, clear permissions, and mechanisms for evaluating outcomes.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation demonstrates the value of connecting models with external evidence. Agentic architectures extend the possibilities by coordinating multiple operations. Enterprise database technologies provide access to structured information and support the consistency and control required by business applications.

Yet none of these components guarantees reliability in isolation.

The Context–Reasoning–Action–Trust framework proposed in this article offers one way to organise the relationships between them. Its central proposition is that intelligent enterprise applications should be evaluated across the entire process: the information they use, the conclusions they reach, the actions they perform, and the controls that govern their behaviour.

The framework remains a conceptual proposal that requires further comparison and validation.

Nevertheless, it highlights an important direction for AI engineering.

The objective should not be to make every system maximally autonomous or to treat every generated answer as evidence of intelligence.

Instead, developers should build systems that can use information appropriately, recognise limitations, operate within defined boundaries, and support meaningful verification.

For enterprise technology professionals, this creates an opportunity to move beyond discussions of model capability and focus on the complete architecture of intelligent systems.

The most useful AI applications will not necessarily be those that produce the longest answers or execute the greatest number of operations.

They will be those that consistently deliver appropriate outcomes under real-world conditions.

The future of enterprise AI will depend not only on what models can generate, but also on what complete systems can justify, verify, and responsibly accomplish.

I Asked My Digital Co-Founder Who to Sell AI Consulting To, and the Answer Was an Order, Not a Market

Everyone hands you a list of segments. The useful part is which one you sell to first, and the rule for that is not margin.

You remember that I want to get a job somewhere, but I am still thinking that maybe it is worth being a classic startup guy and doing AI consulting.

Well, you see, I succeeded in building my second brain, and really all my AIs can do a great deal of the work. I even managed to create a digital co-founder.

So here is what my co-founder said when I asked him what one can make money on. He recommended SMB consulting.

He says the very first companies to sell AI consulting to are US accounting and tax firms with 8 to 50 people. Supposedly they have margins of 50 to 60%, and they will then pull their own SMB clients along with them.

Second in line you should sell to HVAC. I have never heard that abbreviation, but it is plumbers and electricians. And after that, dentists.

Pizzerias are not worth selling to: their margin is small. Whereas those guys above, they have margins of 50% and up.

So: an audit, three grand over 5 days; then building some workflow for them over 10 to 20 days; and then 3 to 5 months of support. And owners of firms with $0 to 100 million in annual revenue close in 2 to 6 weeks.

I remember my experience warming up Chinese and Japanese B2B clients, where you warm them up for a year. In B2B the deal sizes were different, and here in America the deals are, as I understand it, faster.

It is good that I have a crm, but of course I do not have leads like that: no plumbers, no accountants, no electricians.

The rule under the list

Read that list again and notice it is not sorted by margin. HVAC and dentists are both at 50% and up, same as the accountants. If margin were the criterion the order would be arbitrary.

The reason accounting and tax firms come first is stated in one clause and it is the whole insight: they will pull their own SMB clients along with them.

Every accounting firm sits on a book of small businesses. It knows their revenue, their headcount, their pain, and it has permission to call them. Win one such firm and you have not won a customer, you have won a channel. Win an HVAC contractor at the same margin and you have won one customer who knows other contractors socially and has no reason to introduce you.

So the ordering rule, stripped of the industry specifics: sell first into the segment whose customers are your next customers. Margin tells you whether a deal is worth doing. Only the book tells you whether the first deal compounds into the second.

That is a different question from the one most target-market advice answers, and it is the one that decides whether month three looks like month one.

What the ladder is and is not

The offer shape is the standard one: audit at three grand over 5 days, a workflow build over 10 to 20 days, then 3 to 5 months of support.

It is worth saying plainly that this is the least interesting part of the plan. Audit-build-retain is what every consulting practice converges on, for a good reason: the audit is cheap enough to say yes to, it produces the artifact that justifies the build, and the retainer is where the margin actually lives. Nothing about it is specific to AI or to accountants.

Which means it is also not the thing to spend thinking on. If the segment order is right, a mediocre ladder still works. If the segment order is wrong, a perfect ladder sells one deal at a time forever.

The number I distrust most, and why I am naming it

Owners of firms with $0 to 100 million in annual revenue close in 2 to 6 weeks.

My own experience runs directly against that. Warming up Chinese and Japanese B2B clients took about a year per relationship, with different deal sizes attached. I understand that US SMB moves faster, and I have not sold into it, which is exactly the problem: this is a claim about a market I have never worked, carried in from a model rather than from a conversation.

Two more inconsistencies I would rather state than smooth over. “Firms of 8 to 50 people” and “firms with $0 to 100 million in annual revenue” are not the same population; both are in the advice as given, and nobody has reconciled them. And HVAC is heating, ventilation and air conditioning, not plumbing and electrical, as I guessed in the post.

All of the figures above came out of one conversation with my co-founder. That attribution is not modesty, it is the thing that makes them readable: as research they would be unsupported, as a hypothesis with a named source they are testable.

What I am not claiming

No deal has been closed at these prices. No quote has been accepted. The close-time figure has not been tested against a single real conversation. The margins are reported, not verified.

And the honest blocker is not strategy at all: I have a CRM and zero leads in any of the three segments. No accountants, no HVAC contractors, no dentists. A target list without names in it is a hypothesis about a market, not a pipeline.

So the executable next step is not more segment analysis, it is 20 named leads in one segment and a test of the 2-to-6-weeks claim against reality. That is cheap, and it falsifies the most expensive assumption in the plan before anything gets built on top of it.

Which brings me to the actual reason for writing this. Who has experience selling and automating for these audiences? Specifically: does a US accounting firm of that size really introduce its clients, and how long did your first one take to close?

medium.titulo: Moving a Legacy App to React Without a Rewrite
medium.resumo: Standalone React components on a plain URL, mounted into any app. What worked, what broke, and what we’re still fixing.
medium.conteudo_html:
Standalone React components on a plain URL, mounted into any app. What worked, what broke, and what we’re still fixing.

There is no “Migrate to React” button. We checked. 😉

We reached the point where we didn’t want to build another feature in our legacy frontend. New hires knew React, our new product surfaces were heading toward Next.js, and every change to the old code felt like paying interest on a loan we had stopped wanting.

But the old app is a live product. It has real users, real customers and years of behaviour baked into it. This is the story of how we started moving it to React one page at a time, without freezing features and without a big-bang cut-over. It covers the approach, the code, the three problems we hit, and one problem we are still working on.

Why not just rewrite it?

A rewrite is the cleanest answer on a whiteboard. In practice it means months of frozen features while the business keeps asking for new ones, then a risky cut-over day where every forgotten edge case shows up at once.

We also tried the 2026 answer: let AI convert the pages. It was fast at producing code and slow at producing working code. Every generated page still needed someone to review it, compare it against the legacy behaviour, fix the differences and test it again. For a live product with years of quirks, that loop cost us more time than it saved. AI speeds up a file. It does not migrate a product.

What we actually needed was simple to say: new code in React today, running inside the old app, one page at a time.

The three options we weighed

1. Big-bang rewrite. Clean result, months of frozen features, risky launch. Rejected.

2. Publish components as a private npm package. This is the “proper” answer, and we tried it first. Registry tokens, CI secrets, a version bump on every release, reinstall and redeploy in every app, blah blah blah. It works, but every small change to a component turns into a release ceremony across every consumer.

3. Build each component as a standalone bundle on a plain URL. Build the React component on its own, drop the output into the same dist folder the legacy app already serves, and load it with a script tag. Deploy the component once and every page that uses it gets the update.

We picked the boring one: option 3. It is a one-time setup, and after that moving a page is just “build component, mount component”.

The trade-off we accepted is that there is no version pinning. Every page always gets the latest bundle, so we treat the mount() API as a public contract and keep it backward compatible.

Step 1: Build each component as its own bundle

Vite’s library mode does almost all of the work. It can output a single IIFE file that assigns your exports to a global variable, which is exactly what a legacy page can load with a plain script tag.

// vite.config.ts (component repo)
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  define: { 'process.env.NODE_ENV': '"production"' },
  build: {
    outDir: '../legacy-app/dist/widgets', // same dist folder
    emptyOutDir: false,
    lib: {
      entry: 'src/main.tsx',
      name: 'CandidateForm',   // window.CandidateForm
      formats: ['iife'],
      fileName: () => 'candidate-form.js',
    },
  },
});

A few details that cost us time:

  • define for process.env.NODE_ENV. In library mode Vite does not replace process.env.NODE_ENV for you. Without this line React either crashes on process is not defined or ships its development build.
  • emptyOutDir: false. The output folder belongs to the legacy app. You do not want a component build to wipe it.
  • name. This becomes the global. After the script loads, window.CandidateForm holds everything main.tsx exports.

Step 2: Keep the public contract tiny

The entry file exports one function. That function is the entire public API of the component, and every host app talks to it the same way.

// src/main.tsx
export function mount(el: HTMLElement, props: Props) {
  const root = createRoot(el);
  const formRef = createRef<FormApi>();
  let current = props;
  const render = () => root.render(<CandidateForm ref={formRef} {...current} />);
  render();
  return {
    update(next: Partial<Props>) {
      current = { ...current, ...next };
      render();                     // re-render, not remount
    },
    validate: () => formRef.current!.validate(),
    getValues: () => formRef.current!.getValues(),
    unmount: () => root.unmount(),
  };
}

The important part is update(). It calls root.render() again on the same root. React reconciles the new props against the existing tree instead of throwing it away, so typed input, focus and internal state survive. Remounting on every update is the most common mistake in this pattern, and users notice it immediately because their cursor jumps.

Step 3: Inject it into any app

Because the output is a plain script, the host does not need to know anything about React.

<div id="candidate-form"></div>
<script src="/widgets/candidate-form.js"></script>
<script>
  const form = CandidateForm.mount(
    document.getElementById('candidate-form'),
    { values: candidate, onChange: (v) => draft.set(v) },
  );
</script>

Inside a component of the legacy framework it is the same three calls, wired to that framework’s lifecycle:

<template><div ref="host" /></template>
<script setup>
const host = ref(null);
let form;
onMounted(() => (form = CandidateForm.mount(host.value, props)));
watch(() => props.values, (values) => form.update({ values }));
onBeforeUnmount(() => form.unmount());
</script>

Always call unmount() when the host component goes away. Otherwise every route change leaves a detached React tree, its listeners and its timers behind.

Problem 1: CSS leaked both ways

The first page we moved looked broken in both directions. Legacy global styles such as button {} and .form-control restyled our React form. Our CSS reset then broke legacy pages that had never been touched.

The fix was to mount each component inside a Shadow DOM root and ship its CSS inside that root. Styles from the page cannot get in, and styles from the component cannot get out.

// src/main.tsx (isolated mount)
import css from './CandidateForm.css?inline';
export function mount(host: HTMLElement, props: Props) {
  const shadow = host.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
  const style = document.createElement('style');
  style.textContent = css;          // styles live inside the shadow
  const container = document.createElement('div');
  shadow.append(style, container);
  const root = createRoot(container);
  // ...same render / update / unmount as before
}

The ?inline suffix makes Vite import the CSS as a string instead of emitting a separate file, so the component stays a single script.

Gotchas we hit along the way:

  • Portals. Modals, dropdowns and tooltips usually portal into document.body. That is outside the shadow root, so they render unstyled. Point them at a container inside the shadow root instead.
  • Fonts. @font-face rules inside a shadow root are not applied. Declare fonts in the host document.
  • rem units. They resolve against the host page's root font size, not yours. If the legacy app changes html { font-size }, your spacing changes with it.

Problem 2: Legacy submits, React validates

Most pages could not move in one go. A typical case: the form fields and validation moved to React, but the Save button, the API call and the surrounding page stayed in the legacy app. That needs communication in both directions.

We settled on three channels:

  • Down: props at mount time, and update() whenever the legacy side has new data.
  • Up: an onChange(values) callback on every edit.
  • On demand: validate() and getValues(), which the legacy side calls when the user clicks Save.
// CandidateForm.tsx: React owns the fields and validation
export function CandidateForm({ ref, values, onChange }: Props) {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState(values);
  // legacy pushed new data through update()
  useEffect(() => setDraft(values), [values]);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    getValues: () => draft,
    validate: () => validateCandidate(draft),
  }), [draft]);
  const change = (next: Values) => {
    setDraft(next);
    onChange?.(next);
  };
  // ...fields call change()
}
// legacy page: still owns the submit
saveButton.onclick = async () => {
  const { isValid, errors } = form.validate();
  if (!isValid) return showErrors(errors);
  await api.saveCandidate(form.getValues());
};

One trap is worth calling out. Do not feed onChange values straight back into update(). If the legacy side echoes every keystroke back as new props, the useEffect above overwrites what the user is typing. Push new data down only when it really comes from outside, for example after loading a record from the server.

Problem 3, still open: the first load is slow

This is the part we have not solved yet. Each bundle ships its own copy of React and React DOM, so the first page that mounts a component pays for downloading and parsing React. On pages with two different components, the user pays twice.

What we are trying:

  • One shared React runtime. Build components with react and react-dom marked as external, and load React once per page. React 19 no longer ships UMD builds, so this means a tiny runtime bundle of our own that sets window.React and window.ReactDOM, or moving to ES modules with an import map.
  • Preload, then mount on demand. Add <link rel="preload" as="script"> for the bundle, and mount only when the component scrolls into view.
  • Hashed file names with long caching. Because the URL is fixed, this needs a tiny stable loader script with a short cache, which then loads content-hashed bundles that can be cached for a year.

If you have shipped this pattern at scale, I would genuinely like to hear how you handled the first load.

Where this goes next

The nice side effect of this approach is that nothing is throwaway. Every component we move is plain React with a small mount wrapper. When enough of a section has moved, the same components drop straight into the Next.js app, and that whole route is served by Next.js instead of the legacy app. The two apps share the session through cookies, so users move between them without noticing.

The legacy app shrinks one page at a time while it keeps shipping, and there is never a cut-over day.

Checklist if you want to try this

  1. Build each component with Vite library mode as a single IIFE file.
  2. Define process.env.NODE_ENV and never let the build empty the host's folder.
  3. Export one mount() function that returns update, unmount and any methods the host needs.
  4. Re-render on update. Never remount.
  5. Isolate CSS with a Shadow DOM root, and move portals, fonts and rem assumptions with it.
  6. Keep the host in charge of anything it still owns, and talk through props down, callbacks up and methods on demand.
  7. Treat the mount API as a public contract, because there is no version pinning.
  8. Plan for the first load from day one.

How would you cut the first load? Tell me in the comments. 👇

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Amos Kipruto e Hawi Feysa vencem a Maratona de Chicago com recordes pessoais. Veja também como foi a corrida temática do Iron Maiden em São Paulo, os resultados da Maratona de Lisboa e a vitória de Eliud Kipchoge com recorde do percurso na Maratona de Melbourne.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 12 de outubro de 2026

No último domingo, a Maratona de Chicago foi palco de grandes performances. Na prova masculina, o queniano Amos Kipruto venceu com o tempo de 2h01min09s, igualando a marca de Eliud Kipchoge como o quinto melhor tempo da história. A grande surpresa foi a derrota do ugandense Jacob Kiplimo, que vinha de uma sequência de resultados ascendentes, mas terminou na quarta posição. Na disputa feminina, a etíope Hawi Feysa sagrou-se bicampeã com 2h13min33s, após uma acirrada disputa com a queniana Sharon Lokedi. Ambos os vencedores, Kipruto e Feysa, estabeleceram novos recordes pessoais na prova.

Chicago teve um número recorde de concluintes, com 54.592 corredores cruzando a linha de chegada, dos quais 1.491 eram brasileiros. Entre os homens do Brasil, os melhores foram José Eraldo Lima (2h20min34s), Diego Ferrari (2h25min53s) e Jean Nunes (2h31min53s). No feminino, os destaques foram Marilia Serizawa (2h56min39s), Mariana Penatti (2h58min58s) e Talita Brito (2h59min57s). Outro feito notável foi do americano Galen Rupp, que, aos 40 anos, completou a prova em 2h06min55s, estabelecendo um novo recorde máster e terminando na 11ª colocação geral.

A experiência na corrida do Iron Maiden em São Paulo

No sábado à noite, aconteceu em São Paulo a “Run For Your Lives”, a corrida oficial do Iron Maiden. O evento teve um clima mais de show do que de uma prova competitiva, com diversas ativações e uma apresentação da banda cover “The Beast Experience”, cujo vocalista impressionou pela semelhança com a voz de Bruce Dickinson. A largada foi embalada por “Prowler”, primeira música do primeiro álbum da banda. O percurso de 5 km passou por pontos históricos do centro da cidade, como a Galeria do Rock, o Pátio do Colégio, o Theatro Municipal e os viadutos Santa Ifigênia e do Chá. Um ponto de melhoria para futuras edições seria a largada em ondas, para evitar o acúmulo de pessoas no início. A medalha, com o rosto do mascote Eddie, foi um dos grandes destaques.

Resultados da Maratona de Lisboa

A Maratona de Lisboa também aconteceu no fim de semana, com uma chegada apoteótica na Praça do Comércio. O vencedor da prova masculina foi Martin Nsibei Musau, de Uganda, com o tempo de 2h08min07s. No feminino, a vitória ficou com a etíope Meskerem Mamo Hailu, que completou o percurso em 2h28min04s.

Entre os brasileiros, Matheus Pires foi o mais rápido, com 2h36min00s, seguido por Lucas Albuquerque (2h43min47s) e Rafael Gonçalves (2h53min20s). No feminino, a melhor brasileira foi Carolina Andraus, com 3h17min59s, seguida por Beatriz Andrade (3h19min51s) e Adriana dos Santos (3h22min07s).

Última etapa da ASICS Run Challenge

O circuito ASICS Run Challenge, com provas de 4k, 7k e 15k, se aproxima da sua etapa final, que acontecerá em Florianópolis no dia 8 de novembro. O evento, que já passou por Belo Horizonte, Recife e outras capitais, é uma excelente oportunidade para buscar um recorde pessoal. Se você quiser participar da etapa de Florianópolis, pode usar o cupom “CORRIDANOAR10” para garantir seu desconto na inscrição.

Kipchoge vence e quebra recorde na Maratona de Melbourne

Eliud Kipchoge adicionou mais uma vitória ao seu currículo ao vencer a Maratona de Melbourne, na Austrália. A participação do recordista mundial na prova faz parte de seu projeto de correr uma maratona nos sete continentes, sendo esta a etapa da Oceania. Kipchoge venceu com o tempo de 2h09min10s, estabelecendo um novo recorde do percurso. A prova contou com 17.727 concluintes. No feminino, a vitória foi da neozelandesa Camille French, com 2h28min25s.
